fact: Many decisions arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound.
source_span: Many decisions are thought to arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the fundamental decision-making mechanism studied in the article.

fact: In perception, the accumulation of noisy evidence explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
source_span: In perception , the mechanism explains the effect of stimulus strength , characterized by signal-to-noise ratio , on decision speed , accuracy and confidence .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides context for why the study focuses on noise and its effects on decision variables.

fact: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy, and paradoxically, higher confidence according to bounded evidence accumulation models.
source_span: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions , reduced accuracy and , paradoxically , higher confidence .
selection_reasoning: This is a key theoretical prediction that the study aims to test.

fact: The study introduced a novel sensory manipulation that mimics adding unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex.
source_span: To test these predictions , we introduce a novel sensory manipulation that mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex , which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: This describes the main experimental approach used to test the model predictions.

fact: Neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST verified the sensory manipulation increased noise in motion-selective visual cortex.
source_span: which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .

fact: Increasing noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence in both humans and monkeys over a range of stimuli with minimal impairment to accuracy.
source_span: For both humans and monkeys , increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding confirming the model's predictions in two species.

fact: The magnitude of the effects of noise on decision speed and confidence matched predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source_span: The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the experimental results to the theoretical framework.

fact: Decisions that combine information from different sources or over time serve as a model of cognitive function because they are not hardwired or reflexive but experimentally tractable.
source_span: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time are of special interest to neuroscience because they serve as a model of cognitive function . These decisions are not hard wired or reflexive , yet they are experimentally tractable .
selection_reasoning: This explains the motivation for studying bounded evidence accumulation in decision-making.

fact: Psychologists have sought to understand how decision formation gives rise to choice, reaction time, and decision confidence.
source_span: Psychologists have long sought to understand how the process of decision formation gives rise to three key observables ... First there is the choice itself ... Second , there is the time it takes to reach a decision ... Third , decisions are often accompanied by a graded degree of belief in the accuracy or appropriateness of the choice . This belief , referred to as decision confidence ...
selection_reasoning: This frames the key behavioral variables the study addresses.

fact: Bounded evidence accumulation models explain choice, reaction time, and confidence by depicting decision-making as a race between accumulators integrating momentary evidence until a threshold is reached.
source_span: The family of bounded evidence accumulation models ... offers one such framework for linking choice , reaction time and confidence ... These models depict the decision process as a race between competing accumulators , each of which integrates momentary evidence ... The decision terminates when the accumulated evidence ... reaches a threshold or bound , thereby determining both the choice and the decision time . Confidence ... derives from a mapping between the decision variable and the probability that a decision based on this variable will be correct .
selection_reasoning: This explains the theoretical model underlying the study's predictions.

fact: Noise in momentary evidence causes the decision variable to fluctuate, influencing reaction time and confidence especially when signal-to-noise ratio is low.
source_span: The noisiness of the momentary evidence causes the DV to wander from its starting point ... Noise is the main determinant of both RT and confidence when signal-to-noise is low , that is when choices are more stochastic ( less accurate ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the role of noise in decision dynamics relevant to the study.

fact: If noise is selectively increased without changing the expectation of momentary evidence, bounded accumulation predicts lower accuracy with strong evidence, faster reaction times with weak evidence, and increased confidence with weak evidence.
source_span: Specifically , were it possible to leave unchanged the expectation of each sample of momentary evidence while boosting the noise associated with it , then the bounded accumulation of the noisier samples should lead to ( i ) lower accuracy when the expectation of the momentary evidence is strong , ( ii ) faster reaction times when the momentary evidence is weak , and ( iii ) increased confidence when the momentary evidence is weak .
selection_reasoning: This outlines the specific testable predictions motivating the experimental manipulation.

fact: The study introduced a method to selectively increase the variance (volatility) of motion evidence in a random dot motion display without changing its mean motion strength.
source_span: We therefore sought a method to manipulate the variance associated with the neural representation of momentary evidence without affecting its mean. We achieved this with a manipulation of the motion information in a random dot motion (RDM) display, by adding a second level of randomness which increased its volatility but was unbiased with respect to the strength and direction of motion evidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key methodological innovation central to the study's main question and experimental design.

fact: Neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex represent momentary motion evidence and were used to verify the effects of the volatility manipulation.
source_span: We verified that the manipulation has the desired properties by recording from direction selective neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex. Neurons in these areas are known to represent the momentary evidence in tasks identical to those in our study.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important biological context and validation of the manipulation at the neural level, supporting the study's claims.

fact: The volatility manipulation increased the variance of the neural signals representing motion evidence without significantly changing their mean firing rates, especially at weak motion strengths.
source_span: The volatility manipulation produced a small increase in the average firing rate at the low coherences (upper). ... The variance parallels the mean, but volatility has a more marked effect on variance at weak motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This fact captures a principal neural finding that supports the study's hypothesis about noise effects on decision variables.

fact: The study tested how increasing the volatility of motion evidence affected choice accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in both monkeys and humans.
source_span: We then used the volatility manipulation to test the influence of noise on the three observables of choice behavior—accuracy, RT and confidence—in monkeys and humans.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main behavioral outcomes measured to address the study's core question.

fact: Previous methods to increase neural noise in perceptual decision tasks, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation or microstimulation, did not directly characterize the influence of noise on neural signals accumulated for decisions.
source_span: These predictions have not been tested thoroughly, because a controlled method for selectively increasing noise is not known. ... characterization of these effects of TMS and µStim was inferred from behavior. ... psychophysical studies that attempted to increase the noise ... did not characterize the influence of these manipulations on the neural signals that the brain accumulates to form a decision.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides motivation for the study by highlighting limitations of prior approaches.

fact: The standard random dot motion stimulus has a fixed motion coherence for the duration of a trial, whereas the high volatility condition varies the motion coherence randomly on each video frame around a fixed mean.
source_span: In the standard RDM, the coherence, c, is fixed for the duration of an experimental trial ... Here we introduce a second layer of variability, wherein the mean of c is fixed for the duration of a trial but the value of c varies randomly from video frame to video frame ... We will refer to trials that employ this doubly stochastic RDM as the 'high volatility' condition and those that use the standard RDM as 'low volatility'.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key experimental manipulation in a way necessary to understand the study design.

fact: The variance of neural responses to motion stimuli increases more under high volatility conditions, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: The variance of the neural response is known to scale approximately linearly with firing rate ( Tolhurst et al . , 1983; Vogels et al . , 1989; Geisler and Albrecht , 1997; Shadlen and Newsome , 1998 ) . Thus the variance curves in Figure 2C ( lower panel ) parallel the means . The high volatility condition adds to the variance in a manner that is exaggerated at the low motion strengths , consistent with the motion energy analysis above .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key finding about how stimulus volatility affects neural variability, which is central to understanding neural processing of motion.

fact: The firing rate of direction selective neurons in cortical areas MT/MST increases linearly with motion strength in the preferred direction and decreases less steeply in the anti-preferred direction, forming a bilinear function.
source_span: As previously shown ( Britten et al . , 1993 ) , the firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly , on average , as a function of motion strength in the neuron’s preferred direction ( c > 0 , Figure 2C , upper panel , blue trace ) . The firing rate decreases linearly , but less steeply , as a function of motion strength in the anti-preferred direction ( c < 0 ) , giving rise to a bilinear function .
selection_reasoning: This describes the fundamental neural response pattern to motion strength, providing necessary background for interpreting the effects of volatility.

fact: High volatility stimuli increase the variance of motion energy compared to low volatility stimuli, especially at low motion coherences.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy , displayed in Figure 2B , reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli , for all motion strengths ( upper panel ) , whereas the variance is larger for the high volatility stimuli ( lower panel ) . ... Note that the effect is strongest at the low coherences , where the distribution of c in the high volatility condition spans both positive and negative values .
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes how stimulus volatility affects the sensory input variability, which is key to the study's motivation and findings.

fact: The momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide motion discrimination decisions is represented by the difference in firing rates between two pools of neurons preferring opposite motion directions.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e . g . , right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al . , 1996; Ditterich et al . , 2003;
selection_reasoning: This fact defines the neural mechanism underlying decision formation, central to the study's main question.

fact: The visual system blurs rapidly displayed random dot motion stimuli over time, creating the perception of more dots than are actually shown simultaneously.
source_span: The construction of the RDM we use is in video frames displayed every 1/75 of a second . The visual system blurs these images over time , leading for example to the illusion that many more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the nature of the stimulus and its perceptual processing, important for understanding the experimental context.

fact: An established motion filter applied to the stimuli extracts a time-blurred motion signal that approximates the firing rates of direction selective neurons in primate visual cortex.
source_span: The right panel of Figure 2A applies an established motion filter ( Adelson and Bergen , 1985 ) to the example movies parameterized by the low and high volatility traces shown in the left panel ( see also Video 1 ) . The filter extracts a time-blurred motion signal that provides a reasonable approximation to the firing rates of direction selective neurons in the primate visual cortex ( Britten et al . , 1993; Rust et al . , 2006; Hedges et al . , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method used to relate stimulus properties to neural responses, relevant to the study's approach.

fact: The mean motion energy is identical for low and high volatility stimuli across all motion strengths.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy , displayed in Figure 2B , reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli , for all motion strengths ( upper panel ) ,
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies that volatility affects variance but not the mean of motion energy, a critical distinction for interpreting results.

fact: The correlation between neural pools preferring opposite directions is negative because they respond oppositely to fluctuations in the motion stimulus.
source_span: The correlation is negative because the opposing pools respond oppositely to fluctuations in the motion stimulus .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key property of neural population responses relevant to how evidence is computed for decision-making.

fact: The study tested whether increasing the variance of momentary sensory evidence affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence in a bounded evidence accumulation framework.
source_span: In what follows we attempt to ascertain whether a change in the variance of the momentary evidence , introduced by our volatility manipulation , affects decision speed , accuracy , and confidence in accordance with the predictions of bounded evidence accumulation .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main research question and theoretical framework motivating the study.

fact: One monkey and three human subjects performed a direction discrimination task by indicating their choice with a saccadic eye movement to one of two targets.
source_span: One monkey ( monkey W ) and three humans were required to decide between two possible directions of motion and , when ready , to indicate their decision by looking to one of two targets ( Figure 3A ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental paradigm and participants, essential for understanding the methods.

fact: Stronger motion coherence led to faster and more accurate choices in both high and low volatility conditions.
source_span: For both high and low volatility conditions , stronger motion led to faster and more accurate choices .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal behavioral finding establishing the expected effect of motion strength on performance.

fact: High volatility in the stimulus decreased reaction times, especially at low motion strengths, across all subjects.
source_span: The main effect of high volatility was to decrease RTs , particularly at the weakest motion strengths ( Figure 3B , bottom row , red ) . This effect was robust for all three human subjects and the monkey ( Equation 16 , all p<0 . 03 , t-test , H0: β2=0 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a key experimental result linking stimulus volatility to decision speed, central to the study's claims.

fact: High volatility had only subtle and statistically unreliable effects on accuracy for individual subjects in the reaction time task.
source_span: The manipulation affected the accuracy only subtly , and this was not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the RT task ( Figure 3B , top row; for the four subjects: p=[0 . 35 , 0 . 65 , 0 . 2 , 0 . 26] , Equation 17 , likelihood-ratio test ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the limited impact of volatility on accuracy, an important nuance in interpreting the results.

fact: Pooling data across subjects and including confidence tasks revealed a significant effect of volatility on accuracy.
source_span: However , there was a significant effect of volatility on accuracy when pooling data across subjects and including data from the confidence tasks described below ( Equation 18 , p<0 . 0005 , likelihood ratio test , H0: β2=0; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a significant group-level effect of volatility on accuracy, relevant for the overall conclusions.

fact: The volatility manipulation increased the variance of momentary evidence without substantially changing its mean.
source_span: From these complementary analyses of stimulus and neural response , we conclude that the volatility manipulation has negligible effects on the expectation of momentary evidence and more substantial effects on the variance , especially at weak motion strengths .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the stimulus manipulation's effect on the sensory evidence, foundational for interpreting behavioral changes.

fact: The momentary evidence for decision making is modeled as the difference between average firing rates of two pools of neurons selective for opposite motion directions.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e . g . , right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al . , 1996; Ditterich et al . , 2003; Hanks et al . , 2006 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key mechanistic assumption linking neural activity to the decision variable.

fact: Subjects decided the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot display by making a saccadic eye movement to the corresponding target.
source_span: Subjects reported their decision by making a saccadic eye movement to the right ( left ) target for rightward ( leftward ) motion.
selection_reasoning: This describes the core behavioral task used to measure decision-making, essential background for understanding the study.

fact: High volatility in the motion stimulus had only weak effects on choice accuracy but significantly shortened reaction times, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: High volatility had only weak effects on accuracy ( upper ) but shortened the reaction times for all subjects ( lower ) , particularly at the low motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about how stimulus volatility affects decision speed and accuracy, central to the study's claims.

fact: Decisions are consistent with a bounded evidence accumulation model where noisy evidence is integrated until reaching a decision bound.
source_span: The pattern of results in Figure 3B is consistent with the hypothesis that decisions are made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound.
selection_reasoning: This provides the key theoretical framework explaining the decision process, important for interpreting the findings.

fact: Increased stimulus volatility increases the variance of momentary evidence, which accelerates the decision variable's movement toward decision bounds, leading to faster reaction times.
source_span: The important point is that by increasing noise , the volatility manipulation accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable away from its expected value and nearer the termination bounds , hence faster RT.
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight links stimulus volatility to behavioral effects, a core explanatory claim.

fact: Volatility mainly affects reaction times at weak motion strengths where accuracy is already low, explaining why volatility has subtle effects on accuracy but strong effects on reaction time.
source_span: The volatility manipulation mainly affects the weakest motion strengths where accuracy is already poor ... These considerations also help to reconcile the contrast between the striking effects of volatility on RT versus subtle effects on choice accuracy.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the differential impact of volatility on speed versus accuracy, a key interpretive point.

fact: Confidence in a decision can be formalized as the conditional probability that the choice is correct given the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
source_span: Confidence refers to the belief that a decision one is about to make ( or has just made ) is likely to be correct . In the framework of bounded evidence accumulation , it can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the state of the DV , which comprises the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
selection_reasoning: This defines confidence in terms relevant to the study's model, important for understanding subsequent confidence-related findings.

fact: Increased volatility mimics an increase in diffusion rate, which accelerates the decision variable's movement away from neutral confidence, predicting increased confidence at low motion coherences.
source_span: Increased volatility should affect confidence because it mimics an increase in the diffusion rate . At low coherences in particular , its main effect on the DV is to accelerate its exodus away from neutral ( probability correct = 0 . 5 ) to more extreme values . Therefore , we predicted that volatility would increase confidence at low coherences , for the same reason that it speeds the RT.
selection_reasoning: This links volatility to confidence changes, a key hypothesis tested in the study.

fact: A monkey was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering, allowing it to opt out of difficult decisions for a smaller but certain reward.
source_span: Monkey D was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering ... On half of the trials , the monkey had the opportunity to opt out of reporting the direction choice and to select instead a smaller but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental method used to measure confidence behaviorally in a non-human primate.

fact: The high volatility random dot motion stimulus was introduced on a random half of trials after extensive experience with the low volatility stimulus.
source_span: After extensive experience with the standard RDM ( >100 , 000 trials; low volatility condition ) , we introduced the high volatility RDM on a random half of the trials.
selection_reasoning: This experimental manipulation is central to testing the effects of volatility on decision-making and confidence.

fact: The study investigated how high volatility in a random dot motion (RDM) task affects decision confidence in monkeys.
source_span: The main question we wished to address is whether the high volatility condition would elicit fewer sure-bet choices, consistent with greater confidence.
selection_reasoning: This frames the core research question about volatility's effect on confidence, essential for the abstract.

fact: Monkeys performed a direction discrimination task where they could choose a sure bet option for a small but certain reward or make a direction choice for a larger reward if correct.
source_span: The monkey viewed the motion display for random duration, controlled by the computer, followed by a memory-delay period. When the fixation point was extinguished, the monkey indicated the net direction of motion by making an eye movement to a left or right choice target in order to receive a liquid reward, if correct. On a random half of trials, the monkey was presented a third ‘sure bet’ option (red target) during the delay period, which if chosen resulted in a small but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: Describes the key behavioral task and the sure bet option, necessary to understand the confidence measure.

fact: High volatility in the motion stimulus increased the monkey’s confidence, as indicated by a higher proportion of trials in which the monkey waived the sure bet option and chose the riskier direction choice.
source_span: As shown in Figure 4B (lower panel), the proportion of trials the monkey decided to waive the sure-bet option (deciding instead for a riskier direction choice) was greater on the high volatility trials (Equation 19, p<10–6, likelihood-ratio test). Thus, high volatility increased the monkey’s confidence, and did so despite a negligible effect on accuracy.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking stimulus volatility to increased confidence without affecting accuracy.

fact: Volatility did not systematically affect the accuracy of the monkey’s direction discrimination choices.
source_span: Volatility did not affect accuracy systematically (upper).
selection_reasoning: Important to note that confidence changes were not due to changes in accuracy, clarifying the interpretation.

fact: The monkey made rational use of the sure bet option by opting out more often when the motion evidence was weaker or the stimulus duration was shorter.
source_span: In both low and high volatility conditions, the monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression) and for briefer stimuli (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression).
selection_reasoning: Shows that the monkey’s wagering behavior reflected trial-by-trial evidence strength, supporting the confidence interpretation.

fact: When the monkey waived the sure bet and made a direction choice, its accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered.
source_span: When the sure bet was offered but waived, choice accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered (Equation 20, p<10–6, logistic regression).
selection_reasoning: Indicates that the monkey opted out when uncertain, improving accuracy on trials where it committed to a choice.

fact: Human participants showed a similar effect of volatility on confidence, reporting higher confidence ratings for high volatility stimuli, especially at low motion coherence.
source_span: The results from the human observers were similar to those from the monkey... They also reported higher confidence for the high volatility stimuli, and the effect was most apparent for the low coherence stimuli (Equation 21, p<0.0004, t-test).
selection_reasoning: Extends the main finding to humans, supporting generality and translational relevance.

fact: Human participants viewed random dot motion stimuli for 200 ms and reported both their direction choice and confidence by gaze position on targets.
source_span: Subjects viewed random dot motion for 200 ms and subsequently indicated a direction decision and confidence rating by looking at a left or right target (circular arc). The position along the arc indicated confidence.
selection_reasoning: Describes the key method used to measure confidence in humans, relevant for understanding the cross-species comparison.

fact: A single bounded accumulation model can explain how motion strength and volatility affect choice, accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in perceptual decisions.
source_span: So far, the effect of volatility has been described qualitatively. Now we show how a single bounded accumulation model can account for the combined effect of motion strength and volatility on choice, accuracy and RT.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main modeling approach used to explain key behavioral effects, central to the study's principal findings.

fact: In the bounded accumulation model, choice, reaction time, and confidence result from accumulating noisy momentary evidence until a decision bound is reached or the stimulus ends.
source_span: In the model, choice, RT and confidence result from the accumulation of noisy momentary evidence as a function of time, until the integral of the evidence (the decision variable, DV) reaches one of two bounds, or for the PDW and confidence tasks, until the stimulus is curtailed.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a high-level description of the key method and mechanism underlying the study's findings.

fact: The variance of momentary evidence increases with motion strength and is higher under high volatility conditions, especially at low motion strengths.

selection_reasoning: This fact captures a key empirical observation about stimulus noise that motivates the model parameterization and explains behavioral effects.

fact: The model assumes that the brain has implicit knowledge of the accumulated evidence state, elapsed decision time, and how these map to the probability of making a correct choice to generate confidence judgments.
source_span: We can explain confidence if we assume that the brain has implicit knowledge of (i) the state of the accumulated evidence, (ii) the elapsed deliberation time, and (iii) the mapping of time and evidence to the probability of making a correct choice.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the cognitive mechanism proposed for confidence formation, a principal finding relevant to the study's claims.

fact: The model fits to human data show that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in perceptual choices, even when stimulus noise is experimentally controlled.
source_span: These predictions capture the trend well, supporting the notion that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in a perceptual choice, even when noise is under experimental control.
selection_reasoning: This fact states a key conclusion about the determinants of confidence, central to the study's significance.

fact: The influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time, and confidence can be explained by a common bounded evidence accumulation mechanism across tasks and species.
source_span: The overall quality of the fits—across all tasks and both species—indicates that the influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the generality and significance of the main mechanistic conclusion.

fact: Subjects do not appear to adjust their mapping between accumulated evidence and confidence based on the noisiness (volatility) of the stimulus.

fact: Subjects apply the same mapping between accumulated evidence and confidence regardless of stimulus volatility condition.

fact: The laminar dichotomies observed in RSG inputs are similar to those seen in other cortical regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex, suggesting a universal framework for integrating thalamic versus claustral and cortical inputs.
