Thus, our findings may also highlight a more universal framework by which other cortical regions integrate and process thalamic versus claustral and cortical inputs.
selection_reasoning: This fact places the findings in a broader context, emphasizing their general significance.

fact: Anterior thalamic inputs from ADAV to LR neurons in RSG exhibit unique and significant short-term synaptic depression at 10 Hz stimulation frequency.
source_span: 10 Hz anterior thalamic inputs from ADAV to RSG LR neurons were uniquely and significantly depressing.
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a key functional property of the ADAV to LR synapse, central to understanding circuit dynamics.

fact: DS inputs to LR neurons and CLA and ACC inputs to RS neurons exhibit weak synaptic facilitation rather than depression.
source_span: In contrast, 10 Hz DS inputs to LR neurons were not depressing and exhibited weak facilitation... Both CLA and ACC inputs to RS cells were also weakly facilitating.
selection_reasoning: This fact contrasts synaptic dynamics across inputs, important for interpreting functional differences.

fact: Synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is distinct from anterior thalamic inputs to superficial principal neurons in prefrontal cortex and ACC.
source_span: Thus, the synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is unique among the inputs examined here and also distinct from anterior thalamic inputs to superficial principal neurons in PFC and ACC.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the uniqueness of the synaptic property in RSG LR neurons, underscoring its potential functional importance.

fact: Synaptic depression of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons is frequency-dependent, with stronger depression at 40 Hz compared to 10 Hz and no depression at 0.1 Hz.
source_span: ADAV inputs to LR cells do not show synaptic depression at the much slower stimulation frequency of 0.1 Hz, but 40 Hz inputs resulted in stronger depression than 10 Hz.
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the dynamic nature of synaptic depression, relevant for physiological signaling.

fact: Computational modeling shows that synaptic depression of head direction (HD) inputs to LR neurons produces firing rates correlated with angular head speed, generating symmetrical angular head velocity tuning.
source_span: We found that the firing rate of the postsynaptic LR cell receiving HD input via depressing synapses was strongly correlated with angular head speed, giving rise to symmetrical angular head velocity tuning.
selection_reasoning: This fact links synaptic dynamics to a functional coding property, a principal mechanistic insight.

fact: Identical head direction inputs transmitted via non-depressing synapses do not produce firing rates correlated with angular head speed in LR neurons.
source_span: Identical HD inputs transmitted via non-depressing synapses resulted in LR firing rates that were uncorrelated with angular head speed.
selection_reasoning: This fact demonstrates the critical role of synaptic depression in encoding angular head speed.

fact: The angular head speed tuning in LR neurons arises solely from depressing synaptic dynamics, independent of modulation of presynaptic HD cell firing rates by head velocity.
source_span: It is important to note that in our model, firing rates of input HD cells were not explicitly modulated by angular head velocity; therefore, the observed speed tuning resulted strictly from the depressing synaptic dynamics.
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the mechanism underlying the modeled speed tuning, emphasizing synaptic depression's role.

fact: Synaptic depression of head direction inputs may support spatial orientation encoding functions attributed to the retrosplenial granular cortex.
source_span: Taken together, these results suggest that synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns, and potentially supporting the spatial orientation encoding functions attributed to the RSG.
selection_reasoning: This fact states the functional significance and potential behavioral relevance of the findings.

fact: Synaptic depression of head direction (HD) ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the low-rheobase (LR) neuron population in the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG).
source_span: Taken together, these results suggest that synaptic depression of HD ensemble inputs introduces an angular head speed signal into the LR population, producing neurons that are more responsive during faster head turns, and potentially supporting the spatial orientation encoding functions attributed to the RSG.
selection_reasoning: This fact links synaptic mechanisms to the encoding of angular head speed, a core finding relevant to spatial orientation and the function of the RSG.

fact: Anterior thalamic head direction cells display anticipatory firing, becoming most active before the animal faces the cell’s preferred direction, with a mean anticipatory time interval (ATI) of 25–50 ms.
source_span: Anterior thalamic HD cells display anticipatory firing (Blair et al., 1997), a phenomenon where an HD cell becomes most active at a fixed time interval before the animal is facing that cell’s preferred direction... In anterior thalamus, the mean ATI has been reported as 25–50 ms (Taube, 2010).
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines anticipatory firing and ATI, which is central to understanding the study’s investigation of how ATI affects speed coding.

fact: Increasing the anticipatory time interval (ATI) of HD cells improves the timing and quality of angular head speed coding by LR neurons, reducing latency and enhancing tuning independent of lag.
source_span: Increasing ATI from 0 ms (no anticipation by the HD cell) to higher values... improved the lag between LR firing rate and angular head speed, with larger ATIs resulting in shorter latency between the head movement and LR coding of that angular head speed... larger ATIs also improved the angular head speed tuning of LR neurons independent of lag.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing how anticipatory firing enhances the neural encoding of head speed, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Analytical modeling shows that synaptic depression of HD cell inputs onto LR cells leads to angular head speed coding, and anticipatory firing compensates for integration lag, enabling near-perfect speed coding.
source_span: Our analysis allowed us to mathematically derive that LR activity should encode head speed with depressing synapses from simplified HD cells... anticipatory firing compensates for the lag introduced by integration time, leading to a theoretical parameter regime for which postsynaptic speed coding can be essentially perfect.
selection_reasoning: This theoretical result supports and explains the simulation findings, strengthening the mechanistic understanding of speed coding.

fact: Postsynaptic LR neuron activity at lower rotational speeds is proportional to the square of head speed, explaining the parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve.
source_span: Our analysis showed that postsynaptic activity, at least at lower rotational speeds, is proportional to the square of head speed, thereby explaining the concave-up, parabolic shape of the speed-firing rate curve.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key characteristic of the neural response curve, linking physiological data to the underlying coding mechanism.

fact: Heterogeneity in the preferred head directions of presynaptic HD cells creates a tradeoff in LR neurons between encoding head direction and encoding head speed.
source_span: We found that single cell activity in the LR population could encode both head direction and head speed, but there was a clear tradeoff between the two types of information... This tradeoff between directional versus speed encoding was explained by the level of heterogeneity in the presynaptic preferred direction distribution.
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals how input diversity shapes the conjunctive coding properties of LR neurons, a key insight into their functional role.

fact: LR neurons in the granular retrosplenial cortex are unique small, excitable pyramidal cells that are the defining morphological feature of this brain region.
source_span: The small, excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG... Indeed, the ‘granular’ in granular retrosplenial cortex refers to the appearance of these dense small cell bodies in superficial RSG... Thus, LR cells are the defining morphological feature of RSG.
selection_reasoning: This background fact situates the study’s focus on LR cells within the anatomical and functional context of the RSG.

fact: Low-rheobase (LR) neurons are a unique type of pyramidal cell found specifically in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) and are not present in other cortical regions.
source_span: excitable LR cells are unique among pyramidal cells in RSG , and there is no evidence , to our knowledge , for such cells in any other cortical regions
selection_reasoning: This fact provides essential background about the unique cell type studied, which is central to the article's focus.

fact: LR neurons have distinct electrophysiological properties, including low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation, which define their computational role in the RSG.
source_span: The distinct electrophysiological properties of LR neurons , specifically , play an integral role in the RSG’s unique capacity to process anterior thalamic head direction inputs . We have previously reported that the low rheobase and lack of spike frequency adaptation of these neurons are their defining computational features
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key functional properties of LR neurons that underlie their role in spatial processing.

fact: LR neurons are the predominant spatial information-encoding pyramidal cell subtype within the RSG, showing significantly larger responses to thalamocortical (TC) input compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source_span: our results , reporting significantly larger responses to TC input by LR neurons , suggest LR cells are the predominant spatial information-encoding subtype within RSG
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking LR neurons to spatial information processing, a core claim of the study.

fact: The dorsal subiculum transmits allocentric spatial information such as axis and boundary vector signals to LR neurons via projections predominantly to layer 3 of the RSG.
source_span: The dorsal subiculum , which serves to transmit allocentric spatial information such as axis and boundary vector signals ... also precisely targets LR neurons via projections predominantly to layer 3 of RSG
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key anatomical and functional input pathway relevant to LR neuron function.

fact: LR neurons integrate head direction input from the anterior thalamus and spatial inputs from the hippocampal formation via the dorsal subiculum, supporting the retrosplenial cortex’s role in processing directional and distance information.
source_span: Thus , the distinct morphology and intrinsic properties of LR neurons make them ideally suited to integrate head direction input from the thalamus and spatial inputs from the hippocampal formation via the dorsal subiculum . Indeed , this integration of various types of directional and distance information is often stated as the key computational function of the retrosplenial cortex as a whole
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the significance of LR neurons in the core computational function of the retrosplenial cortex.

fact: Thalamocortical synapses onto LR neurons exhibit synaptic depression, which enables LR neurons to compute angular head speed from head direction input.
source_span: We have shown that thalamocortical synapses onto LR cells are depressing ... Our modeling results demonstrate that such depressing synapses allow LR neurons to compute angular head speed from head direction input
selection_reasoning: This fact presents a key mechanistic insight into how LR neurons process spatial information.

fact: The anticipatory firing of head direction cells improves LR neurons’ encoding of angular head speed by reducing time lag and strengthening correlation with head speed.
source_span: We also find that LR encoding of angular head speed is improved by the fact that input HD cells display anticipatory firing ... This improvement not only allows LR cells to encode current head speed with a shorter time lag , but also strengthens the correlation with head speed regardless of lag
selection_reasoning: This fact adds an important detail about how LR neurons achieve precise temporal encoding of spatial signals.

fact: Individual LR neurons can conjunctively encode both head direction and angular head speed through thalamocortical synapses.
source_span: Furthermore , we have shown that this thalamocortical synapse can support conjunctive encoding of both head direction and angular head speed by individual LR cells
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a principal functional capability of LR neurons relevant to spatial navigation.

fact: LR neurons in superficial RSG are predicted to have high firing rates and spike widths intermediate between regular-spiking and fast-spiking neurons, suggesting they form a distinct electrophysiological class.
source_span: LR cells in superficial RSG are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate to the standard ‘broad/narrow’ criteria currently used to distinguish putative RS and FS cells
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a testable prediction about LR neuron properties important for future in vivo studies.

fact: Future in vivo recordings will need to sample extensively from layer 2/3 of RSG to identify the predicted three distinct clusters of spike shapes corresponding to regular-spiking, low-rheobase, and fast-spiking neurons.
source_span: Thus , future recordings will need a large sampling of cells in L2/3 of RSG to provide enough data to identify the predicted three distinct clusters of spike shapes ( RS/LR/FS )
selection_reasoning: This fact outlines the experimental implications and significance of the study’s findings.

fact: LR neuron activity is expected to correlate with angular head speed during spatial navigation.
source_span: we expect LR cell activity to be correlated with angular head speed
selection_reasoning: This fact states a key functional prediction linking LR neuron firing to behaviorally relevant variables.

fact: LR cells in superficial retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) are predicted to have high firing rates and spike widths intermediate between regular-spiking (RS) and fast-spiking (FS) cells.
source_span: First , based on their intrinsic properties ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Brennan et al . , 2020 ) , LR cells in superficial RSG are likely to show high firing rates and spike widths intermediate to the standard ‘broad/narrow’ criteria currently used to distinguish putative RS and FS cells in most cortical recordings .
selection_reasoning: This prediction about LR cell firing properties is a core background and mechanistic claim relevant to understanding their coding role.

fact: LR cell activity is expected to correlate with angular head speed with a relatively small lag.
source_span: Second , we expect LR cell activity to be correlated with angular head speed with a relatively small lag ( Figures 8 and 9 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal functional prediction about LR cells linking them to head movement encoding.

fact: The head velocity tuning curves of LR cells are predicted to be concave up and exhibit approximately quadratic scaling at low rotational speeds.
source_span: Third , we predict that the experimentally observed head velocity tuning curves will be concave up and exhibit approximately quadratic scaling at low rotational speeds , as our analytical work suggests ( Figure 8; Appendix ) .
selection_reasoning: This prediction about tuning curve shape is a key quantitative feature of LR cell coding.

fact: A significant proportion of LR cells are predicted to show conjunctive encoding of both angular head speed and direction.
source_span: Fourth , we anticipate a significant proportion of LR cells will show conjunctive encoding , where both angular head speed and direction are encoded .
selection_reasoning: This conjunctive encoding is a central functional claim about LR cells' role in spatial orientation.

fact: Individual LR cells are predicted to show a tradeoff between directional and speed encoding, allowing the population to comprehensively encode conjunctive speed and directional information.
source_span: A key aspect of this conjunctive encoding , as predicted by our simulations ( Figure 10 ) , is that individual cells will show a tradeoff between directional and speed encoding . As a population , this is likely to allow LR cells to comprehensively encode conjunctive speed and directional information and provide this information to downstream targets , helping with spatial orientation computations within RSG .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how LR cells collectively encode spatial information.

fact: LR neurons in RSG do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 or layer 5 regular-spiking cells, indicating they likely do not provide substantial input to ipsilateral RS or LR cells.
source_span: LR neurons do not synapse onto neighboring excitatory neurons within layers 2/3 ( Brennan et al . , 2020 ) , and no ( 0/9 ) pairs tested in this study between LR and layer 5 RS cells exhibited connectivity ( data not shown ) . Thus , LR cells likely do not provide any substantial input to other LR cells or any RS cells located in layers 2–5 of ipsilateral RSG .
selection_reasoning: This connectivity finding is key to understanding LR cells' circuit role and output targets.

fact: LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG.
source_span: Instead , LR neurons send their axons into the corpus callosum and may likely target homotopic regions of contralateral RSG ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This anatomical fact is important for understanding LR cells' interhemispheric communication role.

fact: Inputs from contralateral RSG preferentially and strongly target RS neurons, with almost no recruitment of LR neurons.
source_span: Our supplementary results ( Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) show that inputs from contralateral RSG preferentially and strongly target RS neurons , with almost no recruitment of LR neurons .
selection_reasoning: This asymmetry in connectivity supports the hypothesis of LR cells transmitting information to contralateral RS cells.

fact: LR neurons in one hemisphere receive unilateral inputs from directional cells in the anterior thalamus to encode information about both the speed and direction of head rotations.
source_span: Thus , we propose the following hypotheses for LR downstream targets and possible function: LR neurons in one hemisphere receive unilateral inputs from directional cells in the anterior thalamus ( Figures 1 , 2 and 6 ) . These inputs are utilized to encode information about both the speed and direction of head rotations ...
selection_reasoning: This is a central functional claim linking LR cells to thalamic head direction inputs and spatial coding.

fact: LR cells may serve to perform a hemispheric switch of rotational speed and direction information by transmitting this information to RS cells in contralateral RSG but not ipsilateral RSG.
source_span: and are subsequently transmitted to RS cells in contralateral , but not ipsilateral , RSG ( Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) . Thus , LR cells may serve to perform a hemispheric switch of rotational speed and direction information .
selection_reasoning: This proposed function is a key implication of the connectivity and coding findings.

fact: RS cells in RSG may use inputs from contralateral LR cells to compare actual head speed and direction signals with motor efference signals, helping to sharpen spatial orientation coding.
source_span: Given the known bidirectional connectivity between secondary motor cortex and RSG ( Yamawaki et al . , 2016a ) , RS cells may be able to utilize inputs from contralateral LR cells to perform comparisons of the actual head speed and direction signal with motor efference signals , helping to sharpen the code for spatial orientation in the RSG .
selection_reasoning: This is a translational implication linking LR cell inputs to motor-related spatial computations.

fact: Projections from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex to RSG avoid laminar overlap with LR apical dendrites and instead target RS apical and basal dendrites.
source_span: In contrast to thalamic and DS inputs to RSG , projections from both the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex avoid laminar overlap with LR apical dendrites , instead projecting to the lower divisions of L1/2 and L5 to target RS apical and basal dendrites ( Figures 3 and 4 , and 6 ) .
selection_reasoning: This anatomical fact distinguishes the input pathways to LR versus RS cells, relevant to their functional specialization.

fact: The claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex are implicated in cognitive and mnemonic functions but also exhibit some degree of spatial information processing.
source_span: Both the CLA and ACC are heavily implicated in a range of non-spatial behaviors often described as being ‘cognitive’ or ‘mnemonic’ in function ... but there is also evidence that these regions exhibit some degree of spatial information processing ...
selection_reasoning: This background fact contextualizes the functional roles of inputs targeting RS cells.

fact: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) plays a key role in contextual fear conditioning by integrating both spatial and non-spatial information.
source_span: This convergence of disparate signals onto RS cells could then serve to support functions that require both spatial and non-spatial integration, such as contextual fear conditioning, a key function attributed to the RSC (de Sousa et al., 2019; Keene and Bucci, 2008a; Keene and Bucci, 2008b; Kwapis et al., 2015; Yamawaki et al., 2019a).
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background and significance about the functional role of the retrosplenial cortex relevant to the study.

fact: Selective ablation of retrosplenial RS cells near the boundary and within upper layer 5 causes contextual fear amnesia, indicating these cells are involved in fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex.
source_span: Indeed, a recent study reported that selective ablation of putative retrosplenial RS cells located near the boundary and within upper layer 5 resulted in contextual fear amnesia (Sigwald et al., 2020), indicating that these cells are involved in the fear-related functions of the retrosplenial cortex (Lukoyanov and Lukoyanova, 2006; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a key functional role of a specific retrosplenial neuron subtype, supporting the study's focus on these cells.

fact: Claustrum (CLA) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) inputs preferentially target layer 3 retrosplenial RS neurons and are implicated in fear-associated behaviors.
source_span: Both the CLA (Cho et al., 2017; Ipser et al., 2013; Vakolyuk et al., 1980; Vetere et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2018) and ACC (Frankland et al., 2004; Han et al., 2003; Steenland et al., 2012) have been heavily implicated in fear-associated behaviors, suggesting again that CLA and ACC inputs to L3 RS cells help to support the role of these neurons in contextual fear conditioning.
selection_reasoning: This fact links specific inputs to retrosplenial neurons with fear behavior, a principal finding relevant to the study's significance.

fact: Retrosplenial LR neurons receive directional and spatial inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum.
source_span: LR neurons receive directional and spatial inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum.
selection_reasoning: This is a core mechanistic finding about the input specificity to retrosplenial neuron subtypes central to the study.

fact: Thalamic inputs to LR neurons exhibit synaptic dynamics that can produce rate coding of angular head speed.
source_span: The synaptic dynamics of thalamic inputs to LR cells can give rise to rate coding of angular head speed in LR cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key functional property of the thalamic-retrosplenial circuit relevant to spatial processing.

fact: Retrosplenial RS neurons respond weakly to directional inputs from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum because their dendrites avoid laminar overlap with these afferents.
source_span: In contrast, neighboring RS neurons in RSG respond very weakly to these directional inputs, as their apical and basal dendrites distinctly avoid laminar overlap with anterior thalamic and subicular afferents.
selection_reasoning: This finding contrasts the input patterns to different retrosplenial neuron types, clarifying circuit specificity.

fact: Retrosplenial RS neurons respond instead to claustrocortical and anterior cingulate inputs.
source_span: Instead, RS neurons respond to claustrocortical and anterior cingulate inputs.
selection_reasoning: This fact complements the previous one by specifying the alternative inputs to RS neurons, important for understanding parallel information streams.

fact: Feedforward inhibition regulates cortical signaling in retrosplenial circuits by modulating responses to thalamic and claustral inputs.
source_span: Matrix TC inputs evoke feedforward inhibition to regulate cortical signaling through both disinhibition (Anastasiades et al., 2021; Delevich et al., 2015) and the disynaptic inhibition of pyramidal neurons (Cruikshank et al., 2012; Yamawaki et al., 2019a; Yamawaki et al., 2019b). Similarly, ClaC inputs invoke feedforward inhibition in several cortical regions, particularly through recruitment of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and, to a lesser degree, FS cells (Jackson et al., 2018).
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights an important regulatory mechanism in the retrosplenial circuit relevant to information processing.

fact: Long-range inhibitory signals from hippocampal CA1 target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a and converge with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs to regulate retrosplenial circuits.
source_span: Long-range inhibitory signals from CA1 of the hippocampus also target apical dendrites in retrosplenial layer 1a, converging with excitatory anterior thalamic inputs, to precisely regulate these TC inputs and establish a hippocampo-thalamo-retrosplenial network (Yamawaki et al., 2019b).
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key circuit interaction relevant to spatial information integration in the retrosplenial cortex.

fact: The study used a mouse model circuit consisting of retrosplenial LR cells receiving input from thalamic head direction cells with short-term depressing synapses.
source_span: Our model circuit consists of an RSG LR cell receiving input from an ensemble of N thalamic HD cells, via synapses exhibiting short-term depression.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a high-level description of the experimental model and approach used to investigate retrosplenial circuits.

fact: Head direction (HD) cell preferred angles shift in anticipation of angular head velocity, effectively transforming the perceived heading trajectory.
source_span: The ATI is defined via the property that when angular head velocity equals ω , the PA of this cell shifts from θ to θ-ωA . Equivalently , we can think of HD cell PAs as static and instead say anticipatory firing effectively transforms the heading trajectory itself: if θTt describes the true angular trajectory , the effective trajectory experienced by our chosen HD cell is:θA ( t ) =θT ( t ) +A⋅θT˙ ( t )
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the core concept of anticipatory firing in HD cells, which is central to the study's background and modeling approach.

fact: In vivo mouse head tracking recordings were used to simulate angular head trajectories for studying HD cell activity.
source_span: To simulate the angular trajectory θTt , we employ in vivo mouse head tracking recordings from the data set CRCNS-th1 ( Peyrache et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key data source and biological system used to model HD cell responses.

fact: The Tsodyks-Markram model of short-term synaptic plasticity was used to characterize synaptic dynamics in the study.
source_span: In the Tsodyks-Markram ( TM ) model ( Tsodyks et al . , 1998 ) of short-term synaptic plasticity , each synapse has a finite pool from which it releases vesicles into the cleft upon arrival of a presynaptic spike .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the main synaptic plasticity model employed to understand synaptic behavior relevant to the study.

fact: Synaptic depression and facilitation dynamics depend on the relative timescales of depression recovery and facilitation decay in the Tsodyks-Markram model.
source_span: In the regime of τd≫τf , depression dominates the synaptic dynamics; conversely , in the regime of τf≫τd , facilitation dominates . Accordingly , the limits τf→0 and τd→0 describe depression-only and facilitation-only dynamics , respectively .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key mechanism of synaptic plasticity dynamics that underlies the study's modeling of synaptic responses.

fact: Parameters for the Tsodyks-Markram model were fitted to experimental EPSP data from thalamocortical stimulation of retrosplenial granular (RSG) low-rheobase (LR) cells, resulting in moderately depressing synaptic dynamics.
source_span: We obtained this parameter set by fitting the TM model response to recorded EPSP amplitudes evoked via thalamocortical stimulation of RSG LR cells with a 10 Hz pulse train ... The resultant TM dynamics were moderately depressing , in accordance with the experimental results .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the model parameters to experimental data, supporting the biological relevance of the synaptic model.

fact: The postsynaptic LR cell was modeled using a morphologically detailed Hodgkin-Huxley conductance-based model including fast sodium, delayed rectifier potassium, and Kv1.1-mediated slow potassium currents.
source_span: We model the postsynaptic LR cell using the morphologically detailed model originally presented in Brennan et al . , 2020 . This model , implemented in NEURON , consists of Hodgkin-Huxley conductances representing a fast sodium current , a delayed rectifier potassium current , and a Kv1 . 1-mediated slow potassium current .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the principal postsynaptic neuron model used to simulate cellular responses.

fact: Each postsynaptic LR cell receives input from multiple presynaptic HD cells, each with a unique preferred angle, to study speed coding and directional tuning.
source_span: Each postsynaptic cell receives input from N presynaptic HD cells , each of which has a unique PA . When studying postsynaptic speed coding , we initially drew the PA of each HD cell uniformly at random from 0 , 2π .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the network input structure critical for investigating postsynaptic coding properties.

fact: The study quantified the relationship between postsynaptic firing rate and head turning speed using time-lagged Pearson correlation and mutual information measures.
source_span: To quantify the extent to which postsynaptic activity reflects head turning speed , we utilized two similarity measures M: Pearson correlation and mutual information . In fact , we used the time-lagged counterparts of these measures ...
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key analytical approach used to assess the functional relationship between neural activity and behavior.

fact: Petal number is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers but varies in the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Petal number, for example, is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers. However, petal number varies in the closely related species Cardamine hirsuta, and the genetic basis for this difference between species is unknown.
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the key biological difference motivating the study and frames the main research question.

fact: Divergence in the floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) explains the species-specific difference in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Here we show that divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator APETALA1 (AP1) can account for the species-specific difference in petal number robustness.
selection_reasoning: This is the principal finding linking a specific gene to the difference in petal number robustness, central to the study's conclusion.

fact: Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 confers robustness in petal number by masking the effects of quantitative trait loci controlling petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: This large effect of AP1 is explained by epistatic interactions: A. thaliana AP1 confers robustness by masking the phenotypic expression of quantitative trait loci controlling petal number in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the mechanism by which AP1 affects petal number robustness, a key insight into gene interaction.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta AP1 fails to complement the function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1, resulting in variable petal number.
source_span: We show that C. hirsuta AP1 fails to complement this function of A. thaliana AP1, conferring variable petal number.
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights functional divergence of AP1 between species, explaining the phenotypic difference.

fact: Upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to the divergence in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: …and that upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to this divergence.
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a genetic basis for the functional differences in AP1, important for understanding evolutionary mechanisms.

fact: Petal number variation in Cardamine hirsuta is maintained despite sufficient genetic variation in natural populations to produce four-petalled flowers.
source_span: Moreover, variable petal number is maintained in C. hirsuta despite sufficient standing genetic variation in natural accessions to produce plants with four-petalled flowers.
selection_reasoning: This fact indicates that genetic variation alone does not explain petal number robustness, emphasizing evolutionary and regulatory complexity.

fact: Petal number is a robust trait in flowering plants, usually invariant within species and higher taxonomic orders, likely due to stabilizing selection.
source_span: Petal number is a robust trait in flowering plants and usually invariant within species and even higher taxonomic orders… suggesting that this trait was canalized during angiosperm evolution to produce a stable phenotype in the face of genetic and environmental perturbation.
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains why petal number robustness is biologically important and evolutionarily conserved.

fact: A stable number of petals helps ensure reliable flower opening and pollinator attraction, supporting reproductive success.
source_span: Petals are usually required to open the flower and to help attract pollinators… therefore a stable number of petals could ensure a reliable display of the reproductive organs and a reproducible cue for pollinators.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides biological significance and motivation for studying petal number robustness.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta flowers show variable petal number ranging from zero to four petals on a single plant, influenced by environmental and genetic factors.
source_span: Cardamine hirsuta flowers display a variable number of petals, between zero and four, on a single plant… This phenotype varies in response to both environmental and genetic perturbation.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the phenotypic variability in C. hirsuta, central to understanding the trait's genetic and environmental regulation.

fact: Environmental factors such as day length, winter cold, and ambient temperature influence petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: Seasonal cues, such as day length, winter cold, and particularly ambient temperature, all influence the number of petals produced in C. hirsuta flowers.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the environmental sensitivity of petal number variation, relevant to the study's context.

fact: Natural genetic variation in Cardamine hirsuta involves multiple quantitative trait loci (QTL) of small to moderate effect that influence petal number in both directions.
source_span: A polygenic architecture of small to moderate effect quantitative trait loci (QTL), that shift the trait in both directions, contribute to petal number variation in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the genetic complexity underlying petal number variation within C. hirsuta populations.

fact: Alleles of large effect and low pleiotropy were found in genetic screens for four-petalled mutants in Cardamine hirsuta but were not detected in natural populations.
source_span: Alleles of large effect and low pleiotropy were identified in genetic screens for four-petalled mutants in C. hirsuta, but were not detected by QTL analysis in natural accessions.
selection_reasoning: This fact distinguishes between experimental mutants and natural variation, important for evolutionary interpretation.

fact: Understanding the genetic basis of developmental traits and their evolution is a major goal of evolutionary developmental biology.
source_span: Determining the genetic basis of developmental traits, and how these evolve to generate novelties, is a major goal of evolutionary developmental biology.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides motivation and context for the study's broader scientific significance.

fact: Developmental systems are generally robust to natural perturbations, allowing normal development despite environmental or genetic variation.
source_span: Developmental systems are remarkably robust to natural perturbations, such that individuals tend to develop normally despite variation in the environment or their genetic make-up.
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the concept of developmental robustness relevant to the study.

fact: Petal number is a robust phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana, with flowers consistently producing four petals across genetically diverse accessions.
source_span: The flowers of A . thaliana and other Brassicaceae species are readily distinguished by their four petals . This phenotype is robust to natural genetic variation; for example , flowers from genetically diverse A . thaliana accessions consistently produce four petals
selection_reasoning: This background fact establishes the baseline robustness of petal number in A. thaliana, which is central to the study's comparison with C. hirsuta.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta shows variable petal number, ranging from zero to four petals, distinguishing it from Arabidopsis thaliana.
source_span: C . hirsuta lacks this robustness and shows variation in petal number . For example , we found similar frequencies of each petal number between zero and four in flowers from 39 C . hirsuta accessions sampled from across the species range
selection_reasoning: This fact defines the main biological difference under investigation, motivating the study of petal number variation and its genetic basis.

fact: The evolutionary transition from a robust four-petal phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana to variable petal number in Cardamine hirsuta is linked to divergence in the floral regulator gene AP1.
source_span: In this study , we investigate the evolutionary transition from a robust phenotype of four petals , typified by A . thaliana , to a variable petal number in C . hirsuta . We show that divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator AP1 can account for the difference in petal number robustness between species
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding connecting a specific gene to the phenotypic difference, central to the study's main claim.

fact: Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 masks the phenotypic expression of all petal number quantitative trait loci (QTL) in Cardamine hirsuta, conferring robustness to petal number.
source_span: This large effect of AP1 is explained by epistatic interactions: A . thaliana AP1 masks the phenotypic expression of all petal number QTL in C . hirsuta and , in this way , confers robustness
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how AP1 contributes to petal number robustness, a key scientific claim.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta AP1 fails to complement the petal number robustness function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1, resulting in variable petal number.
source_span: We show that C . hirsuta AP1 fails to complement this function of A . thaliana AP1 , conferring variable petal number
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the functional divergence of AP1 between species, explaining the phenotypic difference.

fact: Differences in upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to the divergence in petal number robustness between Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: and that upstream regulatory regions of AP1 contribute to this divergence
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the genetic basis of AP1 divergence, important for understanding evolutionary mechanisms.

fact: Petal primordia often fail to initiate in Cardamine hirsuta flowers at early developmental stages, unlike in Arabidopsis thaliana where petal primordia are consistently observed.
source_span: In contrast to this , petal primordia were often missing in C . hirsuta flowers at similar developmental stages . Instead , we observed a flat surface in the second whorl with no indication of outgrowths
selection_reasoning: This developmental observation explains the origin of petal number variation at an early stage, relevant to the study's biological focus.

fact: Auxin activity maxima mark sites of petal initiation in Arabidopsis thaliana but often fail to form or are aberrantly located in Cardamine hirsuta floral meristems.
source_span: At sites of petal initiation in A . thaliana , auxin activity maxima formed in 2 – 3 epidermal cells on the floral meristem flank prior to growth of these cells . However , in C . hirsuta , auxin activity maxima often failed to form on the floral meristem , and instead were either absent or aberrantly located in the first whorl between sepals
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a mechanistic insight into developmental differences underlying petal number variation.

fact: The ptl mutant in Arabidopsis thaliana mimics the variable petal number phenotype of Cardamine hirsuta and shows a similar auxin activity distribution during petal initiation.
source_span: The ptl mutant in A . thaliana mimics the variable petal number found in C . hirsuta and shows a similar distribution of auxin activity during petal initiation as wild-type C . hirsuta
selection_reasoning: This genetic comparison supports the relevance of PTL function to petal number variation, a key experimental insight.

fact: Differences in PTL function are unlikely to explain the variation in petal number between Cardamine hirsuta and Arabidopsis thaliana.
source_span: these results indicate that differences in PTL function are unlikely to account for the variation in petal number between C . hirsuta and A . thaliana
selection_reasoning: This negative result narrows the focus to AP1 as the main genetic factor, clarifying the study's conclusions.

fact: Differences in PTL function are unlikely to account for the variation in petal number between Cardamine hirsuta and Arabidopsis thaliana.
source_span: these results indicate that differences in PTL function are unlikely to account for the variation in petal number between C . hirsuta and A . thaliana .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies that PTL gene function does not explain petal number differences, focusing the study on other genetic factors.

fact: In Cardamine hirsuta agamous mutants, petals replacing stamens in the third whorl have a fixed number of four, while petal number in the second whorl remains variable and lower than four.
source_span: In C . hirsuta ag mutants , four petals replaced the four stamens normally found in the third whorl of wild-type flowers , while petal number remained variable and lower than four in the second whorl
selection_reasoning: This shows that petal number variation depends on floral whorl position and organ identity, a key biological insight.

fact: Ectopic expression of AP1 is associated with an invariant number of petals, whereas endogenous AP1 expression in the second whorl of Cardamine hirsuta is associated with variable petal number.
source_span: ectopic expression of AP1 is associated with an invariant number of petals , whereas endogenous AP1 expression in whorl two of the C . hirsuta floral meristem is associated with variable petal number .
selection_reasoning: This links AP1 expression patterns to petal number stability, highlighting AP1 as a candidate gene for petal number variation.

fact: A genomic construct of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 (AtAP1::AtAP1:GFP) restores four petals and eliminates ectopic flowers in ap1 mutants.
source_span: we used a genomic construct of A . thaliana AP1 ( AtAP1::AtAP1:GFP ) , which was sufficient to restore four petals in the ap1 mutant ... and eliminate the ectopic flowers that characterize the partial loss of floral meristem identity of ap1 mutants
selection_reasoning: This demonstrates the functional role of A. thaliana AP1 in controlling petal number and floral meristem identity.

fact: Introducing the Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 genomic locus into Cardamine hirsuta converts petal number from variable to robust, increasing petal number towards four.
source_span: this transgene was sufficient to convert C . hirsuta petal number from variable to robust , elevating petal number towards the A . thaliana value of four petals
selection_reasoning: This key finding shows that AP1 divergence contributes to petal number variation between species.

fact: Expression of the endogenous Cardamine hirsuta AP1 locus does not significantly change the variable petal number distribution in C. hirsuta.
source_span: the distribution of petal number remained variable in C . hirsuta lines expressing the endogenous AP1 locus ( ChAP1::ChAP1:GFP )
selection_reasoning: This supports the idea that the native AP1 function in C. hirsuta is attenuated compared to A. thaliana.

fact: Allelic variation at the AP1 locus does not contribute to quantitative variation in petal number within Cardamine hirsuta populations.
source_span: We found that none of the QTL mapped to the AP1 locus ... Therefore , allelic variation at AP1 does not contribute to the quantitative variation in petal number mapped in C . hirsuta .
selection_reasoning: This distinguishes interspecies AP1 divergence from intraspecies genetic variation affecting petal number.

fact: The Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 genomic locus canalizes petal number in Cardamine hirsuta by masking the phenotypic effects of at least nine petal number QTL.
source_span: the allelic effects of these 9 QTL were undetectable in the presence of the A . thaliana AP1 genomic locus ... Thus , A . thaliana AP1 canalized C . hirsuta petal number by masking the phenotypic effects of at least 9 QTL .
selection_reasoning: This shows that A. thaliana AP1 stabilizes petal number by epistatically suppressing genetic variation effects.

fact: The Cardamine hirsuta AP1 gene cannot fully complement the function of Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 in ap1 mutants, resulting in variable petal number rather than a fixed four petals.
source_span: we found that the distribution of petal number remained variable in ap1-12; ChAP1::ChAP1:GFP flowers ... mimicking the variable petal number found in C . hirsuta .
selection_reasoning: This reciprocal gene swap confirms functional divergence of AP1 between species affecting petal number.

fact: Expression of Cardamine hirsuta AP1 reduces ectopic flowers in Arabidopsis thaliana ap1 mutants, indicating that AP1 divergence affects petal number independently of floral meristem identity.
source_span: ChAP1::ChAP1:GFP expression was sufficient to reduce the ectopic flowers in ap1 mutants ... indicating that AP1 divergence between C . hirsuta and A . thaliana affected petal number independently of floral meristem identity .
selection_reasoning: This separates AP1's role in petal number from its role in floral meristem identity, clarifying the mechanism.

fact: Petal number varies between zero and four in Cardamine hirsuta, and average petal number is significantly lower in ap1 mutant plants expressing the AP1 gene from C. hirsuta compared to those expressing AP1 from Arabidopsis thaliana.
source_span: Petal number varied between zero and four, and the average petal number was significantly lower in ap1 plants expressing the AP1 genomic clone from C. hirsuta rather than A. thaliana (Figures 3a and 4a, b, Mann-Whitney U test p=2.08e-07).
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes a key phenotypic difference linked to AP1 gene divergence between species, central to the study's main question about genetic control of petal number.

fact: The AP1 gene from C. hirsuta has a reduced ability to promote the formation of four petals compared to the AP1 gene from A. thaliana.
source_span: Therefore, the results of these gene swaps indicate that C. hirsuta AP1 has a reduced ability to promote four petals when compared to A. thaliana AP1.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding that directly addresses the functional divergence of AP1 between species, a core scientific claim.

fact: Differences in petal number between A. thaliana and C. hirsuta are more likely due to differences in regulatory sequences of the AP1 gene rather than differences in its coding sequences.
source_span: Therefore, functional differences in AP1 that are responsible for petal number variation between A. thaliana and C. hirsuta, are more likely to reside in regulatory regions of the gene rather than coding sequences.
selection_reasoning: This identifies the genetic basis of the functional divergence, a key mechanistic insight relevant to the study's conclusions.

fact: AP1 expression levels are significantly lower in floral tissues of C. hirsuta compared to A. thaliana when comparing lines with matched transgene copy numbers.
source_span: We compared AP1 expression between C. hirsuta lines with matched copy numbers of either AtAP1::AtAP1:GFP or ChAP1::ChAP1:GFP transgenes, and found that expression levels were significantly lower in floral tissues of ChAP1::ChAP1:GFP than AtAP1::AtAP1:GFP lines (Figure 4d).
selection_reasoning: This supports the regulatory difference hypothesis by showing expression level differences, a key experimental finding.

fact: The spatial expression domain of AP1 in C. hirsuta flowers is reduced compared to A. thaliana, with C. hirsuta AP1 expression largely restricted to the sepal whorl and not extending into the petal whorl.
source_span: In contrast to this, C. hirsuta AP1::AP1:GFP was essentially restricted to the sepal whorl throughout stages 4 and 5... We found that the expression of A. thaliana AP1::AP1:GFP extended significantly further than C. hirsuta AP1::AP1:GFP (approximately 5 µm).
selection_reasoning: This spatial expression difference is a key mechanistic detail explaining functional divergence and petal number variation.

fact: C. hirsuta AP1 expression is enriched in the regions between sepals, which may be relevant to petal number variation due to the displacement of auxin activity peaks in these regions.
source_span: By co-localizing the expression of both AtAP1::AtAP1:GFP and ChAP1::ChAP1:RFP... we also found that C. hirsuta AP1::AP1:RFP expression is enriched in the regions between sepals... the enrichment of C. hirsuta AP1 in this domain might be relevant for petal number variation in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This links gene expression patterns to developmental mechanisms influencing petal number, a significant biological insight.

fact: Petal number is a robust phenotype in A. thaliana but is more variable (decanalized) in C. hirsuta, with AP1 divergence allowing other genetic loci to affect petal number.
source_span: Our findings suggest that petal number is a robust phenotype in A. thaliana that became decanalized in C. hirsuta, such that AP1 divergence allowed previously cryptic loci to quantitatively affect petal number.
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the evolutionary and genetic significance of the findings, important for the study's broader implications.

fact: Natural accessions of C. hirsuta lack individuals with four petals, and few have an average petal number approaching four.
source_span: A striking feature of this distribution is the absence of natural accessions with four petals... Moreover, few accessions have an average petal number approaching four.
selection_reasoning: This observation motivates the genetic and ecological questions addressed by the study.

fact: Recombinant inbred populations derived from C. hirsuta accessions can produce lines with high average petal numbers, including four petals, indicating sufficient standing genetic variation for this trait.
source_span: These recombinant inbred populations contained a high frequency of lines with high average petal numbers, including four petals... This shows that there is sufficient standing genetic variation to produce phenotypes through recombination that are not observed in natural accessions.
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals the genetic potential underlying petal number variation, relevant to understanding natural variation and evolution.

fact: No difference in seed output was detected between C. hirsuta wild-type plants and plants expressing A. thaliana AP1 with higher petal number under standard growth conditions.
source_span: However, in standard growth conditions, we could not detect any difference in seed output between C. hirsuta wild-type and AtAP1::AtAP1:GFP plants that differed in petal number.
selection_reasoning: This addresses the potential fitness cost of petal number variation, relevant to ecological and evolutionary significance.

fact: In field conditions, C. hirsuta genotypes with higher petal number have a significantly higher outcrossing rate than genotypes with lower petal number.
source_span: Using field conditions to grow two genotypes that differed significantly in petal number... we paternity-tested the progeny of these plants and found a significantly higher outcrossing rate in the genotype with higher petal number.
selection_reasoning: This links petal number variation to reproductive biology and potential adaptive significance.

fact: Petal number is associated with outcrossing rate in Cardamine hirsuta, with genotypes having higher petal numbers showing significantly higher outcrossing rates under field conditions.
source_span: Using field conditions to grow two genotypes that differed significantly in petal number (2.65 ± 0.08 vs 3.45 ± 0.05, Mann-Whitney U test p<0.001; Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), we paternity-tested the progeny of these plants and found a significantly higher outcrossing rate in the genotype with higher petal number (Chi-square test p<0.05, Monte-Carlo permutation test p<0.001, Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Therefore, outcrossing frequency is associated with petal number in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This finding links a key floral trait (petal number) to reproductive strategy (outcrossing), which is central to the study's biological and evolutionary significance.

fact: The gene APETALA1 (AP1) plays a major role in the evolutionary transition from a stable four-petal flower phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana to a variable petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
source_span: In this study, we identified AP1 as a gene of major effect in the evolutionary transition from a robust phenotype of four petals, typified by A. thaliana, to a variable petal number in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: Identifying AP1 as a key gene explains the genetic basis of petal number variation, a principal finding of the study.

fact: Regulatory changes in AP1, rather than coding sequence polymorphisms, underlie the decanalization of petal number in Cardamine hirsuta by relaxing AP1's epistatic control over alleles affecting petal number variation.
source_span: AP1 polymorphisms do not contribute directly to within-species variation in C. hirsuta petal number. Instead, the decanalization of petal number in C. hirsuta involved regulatory changes in AP1 that relaxed its epistasis over alleles that cause petal number to vary.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the molecular mechanism behind petal number variability, highlighting the importance of gene regulation and epistasis.

fact: AP1 genes from Arabidopsis thaliana and Cardamine hirsuta differ in their ability to specify a consistent four-petal number, with this difference mapping mainly to upstream regulatory regions rather than coding sequences.
source_span: We found that AP1 genes from A. thaliana and C. hirsuta diverged in their ability to specify an invariant number of four petals. This difference mapped broadly to upstream regulatory rather than coding regions of AP1, and did not alter the function of AP1 in flower initiation or sepal specification.
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the conclusion that regulatory divergence, not protein function change, drives petal number differences.

fact: Cardamine hirsuta AP1 is expressed at lower transcript and protein levels in floral tissues compared to Arabidopsis thaliana, particularly in regions where petals initiate.
source_span: We showed that differences in AP1 expression are associated with the functional divergence in AP1 between A. thaliana and C. hirsuta. Specifically, C. hirsuta AP1 transcript levels are reduced in floral tissues and protein abundance is reduced in the small regions of stage four flowers where petals initiate.
selection_reasoning: This expression difference is key to understanding how AP1 regulatory changes affect petal number robustness.

fact: Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 expression defines a robust range that buffers petal number against genetic and environmental perturbations, whereas Cardamine hirsuta AP1 expression falls below this threshold, allowing petal number to vary.
source_span: We propose that the expression of A. thaliana AP1 defines a robust range where petal number is buffered against perturbations (Figure 6a). C. hirsuta AP1 is expressed below this threshold, such that petal number varies in response to genetic, environmental, and stochastic perturbations (Figure 6a).
selection_reasoning: This explains the mechanistic basis for phenotypic robustness versus variability in petal number between species.

fact: Introducing the Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 locus into Cardamine hirsuta masks the effects of natural genetic variation (QTL) on petal number, effectively canalizing petal number in C. hirsuta.
source_span: We mapped this natural variation to specific QTL in the C. hirsuta genome and showed that introducing the A. thaliana AP1 locus masked the effects of all QTL. Therefore, petal number was effectively canalized in C. hirsuta via epistasis of A. thaliana AP1 over existing QTL.
selection_reasoning: This experimental result demonstrates the functional role of AP1 divergence in controlling petal number variability.

fact: The evolutionary divergence of AP1 likely exposed cryptic genetic variation in Cardamine hirsuta, contributing to the maintenance of variable petal number within natural populations.
source_span: Therefore, our results suggest that AP1 divergence likely exposed cryptic genetic variation in C. hirsuta that contributes directly to maintaining variable petal number within natural accessions of C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This highlights the evolutionary significance and biological implication of AP1 regulatory divergence.

fact: Petal number is invariant among natural accessions of Arabidopsis thaliana, reflecting robustness to genetic variation, whereas petal number is variable in Cardamine hirsuta.

However, we could change A. thaliana petal number to variable by complementing ap1 mutants with the AP1 genomic locus from C. hirsuta. These flowers mimicked the variable petal number found in C. hirsuta.
selection_reasoning: This contrast between species underpins the study's focus on genetic and regulatory mechanisms controlling petal number robustness.

fact: The temperature-dependent RRV transmission model accurately predicts the geographic and seasonal patterns of RRV disease across Australia.

fact: RRV is endemic year-round in tropical Australia but shows seasonal epidemics in subtropical and temperate regions due to temperature variation.

fact: There is a two-month lag between peak temperature suitability and peak human RRV cases at the national scale.

fact: Adult mosquito lifespan is the primary trait determining the optimal temperature for RRV transmission.
source_span: The optimal temperature for transmission is moderate ( 26–27°C; Figure 3 ) , and largely determined by the thermal response of adult mosquito lifespan ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2 ) .
selection_reasoning: Identifying the key biological trait driving transmission optima is central to understanding the mechanism.

fact: Thermal limits for RRV transmission differ from other mosquito-borne diseases, with lower limits constrained by fecundity and survival at all stages and upper limits constrained by fecundity and adult lifespan.

By contrast , thermal limits for malaria transmission were set by parasite development rate at cool temperatures and egg-to-adulthood survival at high temperatures ( Mordecai et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This comparison highlights unique aspects of RRV transmission relevant for modeling and prediction.

fact: Mosquito life history traits such as biting rate, vector competence, adult mortality, parasite development rate, fecundity, egg-to-adult survival, and development rate depend on temperature and influence transmission potential.
source_span: In both equations , ( T ) indicates that a parameter depends on temperature , a is mosquito biting rate , bc is vector competence ( proportion of mosquitoes becoming infectious post-exposure ) , µ is adult mosquito mortality rate ( adult lifespan , lf = 1/µ ) , PDR is parasite development rate ( PDR = 1/EIP , the extrinsic incubation period ) , N is human density , and r is the recovery rate at which humans become immune ( all rates are measured in days−1 ) . The latter two terms do not depend on temperature . In the full R0 model , mosquito density ( M ) depends on fecundity ( EFD , eggs per female per day ) , proportion surviving from egg-to-adulthood ( pEA ) , and mosquito development rate ( MDR ) , divided by the square of adult mortality rate ( µ ) ( Parham and Michael , 2009 ) .

fact: The study used mosquito fecundity and adult survival data from McDonald et al. (1980) to fit thermal response models for key mosquito life history traits.
source_span: The fecundity and adult survival data in McDonald et al . ( 1980 ) were published as time series of one experimental population at each temperature . The resulting data needed to be transformed to fit the corresponding trait thermal responses .

fact: Mosquito survival data were converted from percent surviving over time into lifespan data for individual females to fit thermal response models.
source_span: For survival , McDonald et al . reported the percent surviving approximately every other day ( hereafter: ‘semi-daily’ ) . We used these data—along with the number of female adults alive on the first day of oviposition at each temperature—to generate a semi-daily time series estimating the number surviving . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we converted this time series into the number of female individuals who died on each day ( i . e . lifespan data ) .
selection_reasoning: Transforming survival data into lifespan data is a key data processing step enabling accurate thermal response modeling.

fact: Mosquito fecundity data were adjusted by binning over gonotrophic cycle durations and weighting by survival to better represent daily fecundity for a non-synchronized population.
source_span: Because the population was synchronized , and because mosquitoes lay discrete clutches of eggs separated by several days ( the gonotrophic cycle duration ) , there were many data points when the populations did not produce offspring . These zero-inflated fecundity data are not ideal for fitting thermal responses . Therefore , after digitizing the semi-daily fecundity time series , we binned periods of several days ( the bin size varied by temperature , since the gonotrophic cycle duration varies with temperature ) and took a survival-weighted average within each bin ( so days with more individual mothers contributing to offspring production counted more ) . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we weighted the values within each bin by the mean number of surviving mothers in that bin . This approach allowed us to more accurately reflect daily fecundity averaged over a non-synchronized mosquito population .
selection_reasoning: Adjusting fecundity data to account for mosquito biology and survival improves the accuracy of thermal response models, a key methodological detail.

fact: The study used the genus name Aedes for mosquitoes despite a recent taxonomic proposal to elevate some subgenera to genus status, reflecting current consensus.
source_span: In 2000 there was a proposed shift in mosquito taxonomy: several subgenera within the genus Aedes were elevated to genus status ( Wilkerson et al . , 2015 ) . This change affected Aedes vigilax and Aedes camptorhynchus , which were called Ochlerotataus vigilax and Ochlerotatus camptorhynchus for a time by some researchers . More recently , there has been a consensus to return to the previous naming system , so we use Aedes here , although many of the papers we cite use Ochlerotatus instead .
selection_reasoning: Clarifying mosquito taxonomy is important background for interpreting species-specific results and literature.

fact: Generation of beta oscillations in motor cortex reduces the probability of accidental movement but compromises encoding of specific movement plans.
source_span: We proposed that the shifts observed in activity of motor cortical neurons caused by generation of beta oscillations reduce the probability of accidental movement in exchange for compromised encoding of specific movement plans.
selection_reasoning: This implication highlights the functional significance of beta oscillations in motor control.

fact: In the neurofeedback-reaching task, monkeys modulated their motor cortical beta power to control a cursor and then performed an arm reach to a peripheral target.
source_span: In the neurofeedback-reaching ( NR ) task monkeys performed neurofeedback immediately followed by an arm reach to a peripheral target ( Figure 1b , c ) .

fact: The beta neurofeedback cursor represented an estimate of the monkey’s motor cortical beta power, updated every 100 ms based on local field potential signals.
source_span: A yellow square beta cursor representing an estimate of the monkey’s motor cortical beta power and one of four beta targets appeared on the left of the screen . As estimates of normalized motor cortical beta power increased or decreased , the beta cursor position increased or decreased on the y axis , updating every 100 ms .
selection_reasoning: Explains the neural signal used for neurofeedback, central to the study's method and findings.

fact: Monkeys successfully ended the neurofeedback epoch by modulating their beta power to hold the beta cursor over a target for 450 ms within 60 seconds.
source_span: Subjects modulated their endogenous neural signals to make the beta cursor hover over the beta target for 450 ms to successfully end the neurofeedback epoch . Subjects had 60 s to reach the beta target with their beta cursor before the trial timed out and the same beta target repeated .
selection_reasoning: Describes the behavioral criterion for successful neurofeedback control, key to interpreting results.

fact: After completing the neurofeedback epoch, monkeys performed a reaching movement to a peripheral target and received a liquid reward upon successful hold.
source_span: Once the neurofeedback epoch was completed the reaching epoch began . The beta cursor and beta target disappeared and a peripheral reach target appeared in a location 6 . 5 cm away from the center target . Once subjects reached the peripheral target and held for 200 ms , they received a liquid reward .
selection_reasoning: Links neurofeedback control to subsequent motor behavior and reward, important for understanding task structure and motivation.

fact: The beta neurofeedback cursor was computed from local field potential signals recorded from selected motor cortex electrodes showing strong beta oscillations and minimal artifacts.
source_span: The beta neurofeedback cursor was designed to reflect endogenous beta oscillatory events in motor cortex . To calculate its position at each time point ( every 100 ms ) , LFP signals from three channels in the most anterior part of the implanted multi-electrode array were manually selected for each subject . Minimal artifacts and strong beta oscillatory activity during the reaching only task were the selection criterion , as in Engelhard et al . ( 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: Provides mechanistic detail on how the neurofeedback signal was derived, relevant for understanding the neural basis of the task.

fact: Normalized beta power was calculated by dividing beta band power (25–40 Hz) by broadband power (1–100 Hz) averaged across selected channels.
source_span: Beta band and broadband estimates were then averaged across channels , and finally a normalized estimate of beta power ( βest ) was computed by dividing the beta band power estimate by the broadband power estimate:βest=13 ∑ch=13 ∑f=25 Hz40 Hz PSDfch13 ∑ch=13 ∑f=1 Hz100 Hz PSDfch
selection_reasoning: Describes the key neural signal processing step that underlies the neurofeedback cursor, important for interpreting the neural control.

fact: Monkey G performed a variant of the neurofeedback-reaching task where the cursor's horizontal position was controlled by normalized 1–10 Hz power in addition to vertical control by beta power.
source_span: Monkey G performed one task variant of the NR task where the neurofeedback cursor in the x-axis was controlled with normalized 1–10 Hz power in addition to it being controlled in the y-axis with normalized beta power , as described above .
selection_reasoning: Highlights an experimental manipulation testing control of multiple frequency bands, relevant to the study's exploration of neural control.

fact: Performance during the beta neurofeedback epoch was assessed by comparing actual beta cursor control to a target-shuffled simulation to determine if control was volitional rather than chance.
source_span: For each session ( typically lasting 10–40 min ) , beta cursor position from the session’s online performance was re-run through a target-shuffled task simulation , designed to assess whether the subjects’ performance during the beta neurofeedback epoch of the NR task was resulted merely from chance fluctuations in beta power or was caused by volitional changes in beta power that were specific for the beta target on the screen .
selection_reasoning: Describes the key method used to validate that neurofeedback control was intentional, critical for interpreting the main findings.

fact: The study used a simulation of a beta cursor task where success was measured by the number of beta targets acquired within a session.
source_span: In the simulation , after the beta cursor entered the beta target and held for the 450 ms beta target hold time , an average arm-reaching time , the constant reward time , and the constant inter-trial interval time transpired to simulate the natural pacing of the task . At the end of the simulation , a metric of chance performance was the mean number of successful beta targets acquired over the length of the session .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the core behavioral task and performance metric used in the study, which is central to understanding the experimental design and findings.

fact: One hundred simulations were run per session to generate a distribution of rewarded targets per minute, which was used to calculate z-scores for actual performance.
source_span: One hundred simulations were run per session ( each session ~10–40 min ) yielding a distribution of rewarded targets/minute . The mean and standard deviation of the distribution was calculated , and used to z-score the actual number of rewarded trials .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the method used to quantify performance relative to chance, a key analytic approach relevant to the study's conclusions.

fact: Beta power was analyzed using detrended spectrograms aligned to movement onset to remove the typical 1/f trend in neurological signals.
source_span: In Figure 1d , a movement-onset aligned , detrended spectrogram ( window size is 200 ms , step size is 10 ms , multi-taper method with five tapers ) is plotted from 1 s before movement onset to 0 . 75 s after movement onset . The spectrogram estimate was detrended by first estimating power as a linear function of frequency ( power = m*frequency + b ) using all trials and timepoints as data to fit m , b in the linear regression . Then , the estimated power from the linear regression was subtracted from the computed spectrogram , effectively flattening the typical 1/f trend exhibited by neurological signals .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method for analyzing neural beta oscillations, which is central to the study's investigation of beta power dynamics.

fact: Normalized beta power traces were computed during the neurofeedback and reaching epochs to characterize beta activity related to task performance.
source_span: In Figure 2a–c , normalized beta power traces are shown for the last 1000 ms of the neurofeedback epoch through the first 500 ms of the reaching epoch . These are computed the same way as detailed above in ‘calculation of beta neurofeedback cursor’ , except that they are not transformed from normalized beta power to the cursor position and they are calculated at time steps of 10 ms instead of 100 ms .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the measurement of beta power dynamics during key task periods, which is important for linking neural activity to behavior.

fact: Beta oscillatory events were identified by filtering local field potentials at 25–40 Hz and applying an amplitude threshold based on the 60th percentile of rewarded trials' amplitude distribution.
source_span: To determine when the beta oscillatory events occurred , the following procedure was applied . The local field potential ( LFP ) signal from one of the electrodes used in the neurofeedback task was selected , and filtered at 25–40 Hz with a fifth order Butterworth filter . The amplitude of the filtered signal was estimated with the Hilbert transform . Each day , a distribution of amplitude values was computed by aggregating all rewarded trials from that day . A threshold was set at the 60th percentile of the resultant distribution .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key method for detecting beta oscillations, which is fundamental to the study's analysis of beta activity.

fact: Beta oscillatory events shorter than 125 ms were excluded to ensure that only sustained beta oscillations lasting at least 3–4 cycles were analyzed.
source_span: Then , the length of each block of uninterrupted '1s' was computed , and if the block was longer than 125 ms ( so the oscillatory episode lasted at least 3–4 cycles as described in Murthy and Fetz ( 1996a ) ; Sherman et al . , 2016 ) , the block remained as is . If the block was less than 125 ms , all points in the block were changed back to '0s' .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the criteria for defining meaningful beta oscillations, which impacts the interpretation of neural activity.

fact: A hand speed threshold of 3.5 cm/sec was used to distinguish slow from fast movement timepoints, optimizing classification of spiking patterns in monkeys during the task.
source_span: Throughout the study slow and fast timepoints are distinguished . A threshold of 3 . 5 cm/sec applied to hand speed was used to separate slow from fast . This threshold was chosen because using it yielded the best discrete classifier performance separating slow spiking patterns from fast spiking patterns in Monkeys G and C’s CO task in comparison with other thresholds ( data not shown ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important context for behavioral-neural analyses, linking movement speed to neural firing patterns.

fact: Movement onset time during the arm-reaching epoch was defined as the time when projected hand speed first exceeded 20% of its peak value, allowing consistent comparisons across targets and animals.
source_span: To compute movement onset time for the arm-reaching epoch in the NR task , we used a method inspired by Churchland and Shenoy ( 2007 ) . First , the x and y cursor velocity over the course of the reach ( t x 2 ) was projected onto a unit vector pointing from the center to peripheral target . The norm of the projected cursor velocities yielded a single time series of projected speed ( t x 1 ) . The index and value of maximum projected hand speed was computed and called ( i , M ) . Starting at i , we scanned backwards in time ( i-1 , i-2 , … ) until the value of the projected hand speed fell below 20% of the peak hand speed ( 0 . 2*M , see Figure 1f ) . This timepoint was called the movement onset time and was used because it allowed for comparisons across different reach targets , animals , and experimental setups without having to define absolute hand velocity cutoffs .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key behavioral metric used to align neural and movement data, critical for interpreting task-related neural dynamics.

fact: Movement onset time was used as a standardized timepoint to compare reach behaviors across different targets, animals, and experimental setups without relying on absolute hand velocity cutoffs.
